sections.heading: Company paintings
sections.content: Built entirely of white marble, Victoria Memorial represents a unique combination of classical European architecture and Mughal motifs. The domed and white marble museum sprawls over acres of land and is set in a landscaped garden at the southern side of Kolkata. Designed after the Taj Mahal in Agra, it has a vast collection of pictures, statues, manuscripts, letters etc, relating to the Nawabi and British times in Bengal. The memorial was the brainwave of Lord Curzon, who in 1901, felt that the recently departed Queen Victoria, required a suitable monument in her memory. Completed in 20 years, the Prince of Wales formally inaugurated it in 1921. Set amidst acres of lawns, and fountains the memorial consists of numerous features including Italian-style statues over its entrances, Mughal domes in its corners and tall elegant open curved pillars along its sides. There are about 3000 exhibits in 25 galleries in a chamber beneath the dome. A bronze statue of Queen Victoria sits enthroned at the entrance marble staircase wearing the regal Order of the Star of India. The entrance dome is deeply engraved with the text of Queen Victoria's imperial proclamation speech. Inside the memorial there is a remarkable collection of artifacts depicting British Imperialism. In the Royal Gallery there are many oil paintings illustrating episodes from Queen Victoria's long, eventful life and reign. The memorial is famous for its exhibits of Indian and Western

sections.heading: West Bengal- Monument- Dakshineshwar
sections.content: Dakshineshwar in Hooghly district is known for its Kali temple, being associated with Ramakrishna Paramahamsa in the 19th century who was the spiritual Guru of Swami Vivekananda. Located in nearby Kolkata, is the well known Kalighat temple also dedicated to Kali. The temple although erected in 1855, is representative of Bangla temple architecture, with a cluster of towers, with a central dome towering above the rest, with a two layered roof - one superimposed on the other, with four domes in four corners, with a corridor having curvilinear roof in between each pair of domes and the walls are plastered.

sections.heading: Terracotta Temples, Bishnupur
sections.content: Bishnupur boasts of thirty temples built between seventeenth and eighteenth century. It is a treasure-trove of terracotta sculptures. The temples are built mostly of brick and at times, of laterite. The architecture is modeled on the pattern of Bengali huts built of bamboo and mud and thatched roofed. For almost a thousand years it was the capital of the Malla kings of Mallabhum, of which Bankura was a part. The temples are dedicated to Radha and Krishna. Here, royal architects and craftsmen of Bengal have poured all their talents into the red laterite soil found here, and the result was one of the most beautiful cities in the world of its time built of terracotta. Apart from the temples, terracotta pottery, artifacts and even jewellery from Vishnupur is famous. The potters here derive their inspiration from the glorious history of kings, soldiers and wars. Rasmancha is the oldest brick temple having a unique style with a cubic shrine, pillared corridors on three sides and a pyramidal roof. The temples built after this Pancharatna Temple , the Radha Shyama Temple and the Keshta Raya Temple are the best examples of terracotta architecture. The temple built of bricks has an exterior and interior clad with high quality, densely sculpted, terracotta panels. It is a Pancharatna with a main tower and four small towers in the four corners. The temple has a square plan with porches on all four sides and a three-arch entrance, on each of the four sides. The ceiling is is in the form of a dome with a terracotta finish having Islamic influence with a terracotta finish that is not seen in any other temple. Most of the sculptures are of Krishna. There are Rasa mandalas with Krishna, Radha and gopis. Jorebangla Temple has two traditional Bengali huts placed together and the sloping split roof called Bangaldar roof. Madanmohan temple built in 1694 CE in the Ekaratna style, a square flat-roofed building with carved cornices, surmounted by a pinnacle. Impressive carvings on the walls depict scenes from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and the Puranas. The temples at Bishnupur are mostly of Ekaratna type with a single tower upon a sloping roof and a square cell (Garbhagriha) flanked by a porch on each side with three cusped arches.

sections.heading: West Bengal- Monument- Shantiniketan
sections.content: Shantiniketan, was founded in 1863 by Maharishi Devendranath Tagore and it was his son, Rabindranath who converted it into an experimental open-air school with just five students in 1901. Gradually it developed into the Vishva Bharati University which became an important centre of learning including arts. The Vishva Bharati campus is an interesting synthesis of murals, frescoes, paintings and sculptures. Rabindranath Tagore, Nandlal Bose, Ramkinkar Baij, amongst other prominent personalities in education built this educational movement. The Uttarayan complex where Tagore lived has a number of architecturally unique buildings such as the Udayana, Konark, Shyamali, Punascha and Udichi. About 3 km from Shantiniketan is Sriniketan which was Tagores vision of rural expansion. Sriniketan focuses on agriculture, adult education, village welfare, cottage industries and handicrafts. Rural co-operative stores sell the handicrafts produced in neighbouring villages, such as - batik, kantha embroidery, weaving, bell metal products, dhokra metalware, leather goods and terracotta pottery.etc.

sections.heading: Kalighat Paintings
sections.content: Tradition of Kalighat paintings in Bengal has the genesis from the place where the artists originally set up their practice - around the Kalighat temple in Kolkata. Scroll painters-cum-potters migrated from rural Bengal to the city of Calcutta in the nineteenth century and created this art on mill-made paper with watercolours. Kalighat paintings were mainly depictions of Hindu gods and goddesses including their various incarnations (avatars). But gradually the influence expanded and Kalighat paintings became a reflection of the society of their time. The artists used this medium to record their impressions of the dynamic social environment they lived in. Calcutta, the capital of British India served as the inspiration for these artists. They turned their satirical gaze towards a changing society, changing lifestyles and industrial progress. The Indian art scene, in particular, was under the threat of being swept by the wave of westernisation. Decorative Indian Art was being tarnished and corrupted beyond recognition. The survival of traditional Indian arts therefore became a prime concern. Local traditions suddenly assumed vital importance and there was an acute need for protecting, documenting and reviving rural art. This largely led to Kalighat Paintings being given the importance due to them.

sections.heading: West Bengal- Handicrafts- Clay and Terracotta
sections.content: Krishnagar in Nadia district of West Bengal is famous for its sharply chiseled and finely shaped dolls of clay which are moulded by hand and then fired. The dolls have finely detailed depictions of Brahmins, snake charmers, jewellers, women, blacksmiths, potters etc. The toys are extremely shiny because of the application of extract of tamarind seeds.

sections.heading: West Bengal- Handicrafts- Terracotta
sections.content: West Bengal has some of the largest collection of the finest specimens of temple terracotta panels. Some of the best examples of this craft are seen in Murshidabad, Birbhum, Jessore, Bansberia (Hooghly) and Digha. The use of terracotta plaques, medallions and wall panels as integral part of architecture is undoubtly a speciality of West Bengal. The themes of these art pieces are drawn from epics and old legends. The style of the art is however essentially folk with very expressive traditional designs. The plasticity of the material is very skillfully used.

sections.heading: Kantha Embroidery
sections.content: Kantha evolved out of necessity to drape or protect against cold. Kontha in Sanskrit means rags. It can rightly be called the recycling art. The precious silks and muslins when became worn-out, women instead of throwing them away, piled them in layers and stitched. The Kantha narrates a story, the emotions and the life of the artist. The process involves laying the worn clothes in layers and stitching them together. Though the stitch used is variations of running stitch, the motifs can range from being simple to very intricate. sections.heading: Sholapith craft
sections.content: The reed of shola, a herbaceous plant growing wild in the wetlands of West Bengal is used for making decorative objects in the state. The craftsmen known as malakars transform the light and lustrous inner portions of the plant into minutely and delicately worked decorations for the deities particularly that of Durga. They use a special kind of knife called Kath to shave the stalk. Shaving is done very carefully without damaging the stalk as the main motive is to expose the white core. They also design garlands, floral bonquets and mobiles as well as the beautiful headgears (Mukuts) worn by Bengali brides and grooms on their wedding day.

sections.heading: West Bengal- Handicrafts- Stonecraft
sections.content: Midnapur district is an important traditional region for stoneware with Simulpal as the main centre. The practising craftsmen are karga, bhumif and karmakar. The stone here is called potstone and actually it is phyllite. It is reddish and greenish in one quarry but greyish and blackish in another. The former is more brittle and is more widely used as it is softer. The articles made here are mainly used for daily household needs with the exception of a few decorative items.

sections.heading: West Bengal- Handicrafts- Masks
sections.content: In West Bengal the wooden masks are an important part of the attire of the Gambhira dancers. The Purulia Chhou masks represent gods and goddesses and mark the beginning of spring when episodes from epics are performed. These simple masks are made of papier mache and have a quality of earthiness about them.

sections.heading: West Bengal- Handicrafts- Baluchar Silk
sections.content: The Baluchar silk sarees originate from a place of the same name in the district of Murshidabad and had its heyday under the patronage of royalty and nobility. Very colourful, a real traditional Baluchar is said to have 17 colours in it with embroidered designs (butis) woven all over. It is a plain woven fabric brocaded with untwisted silk thread with unique designs. The pallu which is the main piece of a large panel with mangoes in the centre is bordered by diverse designs ranging from scenes depicting the royal court to birds, flowers and historical monuments. The sarees are always in dark rich shades, particularly red, purple and browns. The simpler baluchar has small dots or flowers all over with a flowery border and mango patterns (ambi) in the pallu.

sections.heading: Scroll Paintings
sections.content: The craft of scroll painting in West Bengal is traditional and the painters of this type of scroll pat painting are known as patidars. They take a very long old piece of cloth on which they lay black earth paste often mixed with cowdung. When this cloth is dried, a coating of lac is given to stiffen it and fill up the porous surface. The outlines of the figures are in lamp black or red and the bodies are filled with vegetable dyes which retain their brilliance over a long period. The figures are symbolic and bold, vigorous and spontaneous in style.

sections.heading: West Bengal- Handicrafts- Durries
sections.content: In Darjeeling, the local Bhutias traditionally weave durries. Their designs show strong Tibetan influences with dragons, clouds, etc. Around Shantiniketan, where poet Rabindranath Tagore had initiated a revival of handicrafts, interesting experiments were made using jute yarn for the weft and cotton for the warp with local folk designs from the old kantha embroideries. These designs however take on a new look when presented in this broad weave. The loom is a simple bamboo frame and the panja is used to bear the weft thread.

sections.heading: West Bengal- Handicrafts- Conch shell
sections.content: West Bengal has a heritage of crafts that is based on the resources of the sea and on land locked traditions. In Kolkata and Midnapore, sankharis or conchshell workers practice this age-old craft. With an expertise honed to near perfection by long years of experience, they slice the radiating conchshells with simple hand tools and fashion bangles, bracelets and a range of ornaments. Ritualistically, conchshell bangles, once worn, are not to be discarded by Bengali women during the lifetime of their husbands. Along with shell articles cutlery such as spoons, forks, knives, small plates, and jewellery are also produced.

sections.heading: Paintings- The Bengal School: Artists of Bengal
sections.content: The Bengal School was a highly influential style of art that flourished in India during the British Raj in the early 20th century. It was associated with Indian nationalism, but was also promoted and supported by many British arts administrators. EB Havell, a connoisseur and promoter of Indian art, was appointed Principal of Calcutta Art School in 1896. In 1905 Havell persuaded Abanindranath Tagore to join the School as Vice-Principal and together they introduced traditional Indian techniques of art in the school. Nandalal Bose, Surendranath Kar, Asit Kumar Halder, joined as disciples of Abanindranath and helped introduce a new revivalist style of painting. In the nationalistic fervour of the time it gained tremendous popularity and spread all over India. Abanindranath Tagore (1871-1951) Abanindranath Tagore was born in Jorasanko, Kolkata on 7 August 1871. He attended the studio of Charles Palmer, an English painter, for instructions in oil paintings and portraiture. In 1895 he painted the KrishnaLila series, which display a unique blend of both European and Indian, styles. Taikan, a Japanese painter taught Abanindranath the watercolour and wash technique and how to wield the brush with a light touch and of the evocative powers of gestures. He was able to incorporate this learning into his Omar Khayyam series (1906-08). Abanindranath, the painter was established as the creator of a new national vocabulary in art and he helped to regenerate the decadent art and aesthetic scene in India. The Indian Society of Oriental Art was established to promote the Abanindranath-style on the national plane. Abanindranths best-known painting, Bharat Mata (mother India),shows her depicted as a young woman, portrayed with four arms like a Goddess holding objects symbolic of India's national aspirations. It was his brush, which first gave convincing proof that the Indian artist had his own contribution to make to the world of painting. Rabindranath Tagore (1861-1941) The Nobel laureate had no formal training in art and yet succeeded in producing more than 2500 works of art within a decade. Over 1500 of them are preserved in Viswa-Bharati, Shantiniketan. Evidently, in his quest for newer forms of expression in terms of line, form and colour, Tagore attempted to do something different from what he did in his literary works. If he sought peace and enlightenment in his songs, he wanted to explore darkness and mystery in his drawings. This puzzled and thrilled the Indian art lovers and connoisseurs. With the passage of time, critics and art lovers discovered in these outpourings of his fanciful mind, a more modern Tagore than they see elsewhere. The works of Jamini Roy (1887-1972) are among the most recognizable of Indian paintings. Roy was a very important Indian artist of the twentieth century. His works have since been declared as national treasures of India and are gaining international acclaim as well. One can see the considerable influence of Bengali tradition in his works, even when the portrayal is of European saints. Roy was trained in his formative period in the Bengal school style of painting and his painting represented as much a revival of folk art as a rebellion against the delicate drawing and hazy colors of the Bengal school. He abandoned the three-dimensional modulation, that is to say, the stress on perspective and light and shade of naturalistic western art. Instead, he took to the two-dimensional format of flat colouring and undulated outline of the folk tradition. He created out of the folk mannerism a more sophisticated and harmonious form of painting which expressed a new kind of simple beauty while retaining a kind of Indianness.

sections.heading: West Bengal- Festivals- Durga Puja
sections.content: The most important and the most popular of all festivals of Bengal is the Durgapuja. It is celebrated throughout the state, but with great grandeur in Kolkata. There are some ancestral houses in Kolkata where Durgapuja is being observed over decades and even over centuries. Consisting of series of rituals this five day long homecoming welcome of Goddess Durga is close to everyones heart and soul in Bengal. Festival preparations begin a month or two in advance. The festival starts with Mahalaya, the first phase of the waxing moon in Aswin. Thousands offer prayers to their ancestors at the city's river banks, a ritual called Tarpan. After the three days of Puja, in Dashami, the tenth and the last day, a tearful farewell is offered to the Goddess. The images are carried in processions around the locality and finally immersed in a nearby river or lake. Vijaya Dashami is an event celebrated all over the country. The festive mood builds up as drummers (Dhakis) beat feathered drums. The construction of images Kolkata, is famous as a place for expert artisans who use clay modeling to build the images of Durga, Mahisasur, Kartik, Ganesh, Saraswati and Lakshmi. This is a wonderful form of art and part of a deep rooted culture. Another group of people start building a covered huge stage pandal with paper, wood, bamboos, clothes and other materials. They come up with beautiful structures, most of the times they are so beautiful and real that, it is tough to believe that these are made for only couple of days or a week. The inauguration starts on Mahashasthi. The main puja is for three days - Mahasaptami, Mahaastami, Mahanavami. The puja rituals are long and very detailed and complicated. Three days of mantras and shlokas and arati and offerings - needs an expert priest to do this kind of puja. The Story of Durga Puja The story goes that Mahisasur, the Buffalo Demon, through years of praying, received blessing from Lord Brahma, that no power can kill him which means he is invincible. But once gaining this power he started ravaging the whole world by killing people. And finally he wanted to uproot the Gods too. The Gods, in dismay, combined their powers to create a beautiful maiden, and each placed his or her most potent weapon in one of her ten hands riding a lion. Her return in each year in the month of aswin (September-October) commemorates Rama's invocation of the goddess Durga before he went into battle with Ravana. The traditional image of Durga in Bengal follows the iconographic rules of the shastras. It is similar to the Durga of Aihole and of Mahabalipuram (seventh century). The tableau of Durga with her four children - Kartik, Ganesh, Saraswati and Lakshmi, representing respectively the Protector, the Initiator of the puja, Knowledge and the Provider - signifies the complete manifestation of the goddess.
